title: Human Physiology
description: Neurons and the nervous system, muscle, circulation, breathing, digestion, the kidney, homeostasis, hormones, immunity and reproduction, at introductory-biology depth.

cards.title: Which ion, leaking out through channels that stay open at rest, is mainly responsible for a neuron's negative resting potential?
cards.body:
$\ce{K+}$ (potassium)

$\ce{K+}$ is concentrated inside the cell, so it diffuses out through open **leak channels** and leaves the inside negative, at about $-70\,\mathrm{mV}$ (typically $-60$ to $-80\,\mathrm{mV}$).

Why: the $\ce{Na+}$/$\ce{K+}$ pump maintains the gradients, with high $\ce{K+}$ inside and high $\ce{Na+}$ outside.
Watch out: $\ce{Na+}$ leaks in too, but much more slowly, so the resting potential sits close to the $\ce{K+}$ equilibrium potential.
cards.searchQuery: resting membrane potential potassium leak channels neuron

cards.title: When a neuron reaches threshold, influx of which ion through voltage-gated channels causes the rising phase of the action potential?
cards.body:
$\ce{Na+}$ (sodium)

At threshold (often about $-55\,\mathrm{mV}$), voltage-gated $\ce{Na+}$ channels open and $\ce{Na+}$ rushes in, making the inside positive. Then the $\ce{Na+}$ channels inactivate and voltage-gated $\ce{K+}$ channels open. $\ce{K+}$ flows out (the falling phase), and the membrane briefly dips below rest (undershoot).

Inactivated $\ce{Na+}$ channels cause the **refractory period**, which is why signals travel in one direction.

Watch out: the rising phase is $\ce{Na+}$ entering; the falling phase is $\ce{K+}$ leaving.
cards.searchQuery: action potential rising phase sodium voltage-gated channels

cards.title: In myelinated axons, action potentials are regenerated only at the gaps between myelin segments. What is this jumping conduction called?
cards.body:
Saltatory conduction

The name comes from the Latin word for "to leap". The gaps are the **nodes of Ranvier**, where voltage-gated $\ce{Na+}$ channels cluster. Myelin makes conduction much faster than in an unmyelinated axon of the same diameter.

Myelin comes from Schwann cells in the PNS and from oligodendrocytes in the CNS.

Example: multiple sclerosis destroys CNS myelin and slows or blocks signals.
cards.searchQuery: saltatory conduction myelin nodes of Ranvier

cards.title: When an action potential reaches an axon terminal, influx of which ion triggers synaptic vesicles to release neurotransmitter?
cards.body:
$\ce{Ca^2+}$ (calcium), entering through voltage-gated $\ce{Ca^2+}$ channels

The vesicles fuse with the presynaptic membrane (**exocytosis**). The neurotransmitter then diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds receptors, often ligand-gated ion channels, on the postsynaptic cell.

Watch out: it is $\ce{Ca^2+}$ entering the terminal, not $\ce{Na+}$, that triggers release.
cards.searchQuery: synaptic vesicle release calcium influx axon terminal

cards.title: In skeletal muscle, $\ce{Ca^2+}$ binds which protein, shifting tropomyosin off the myosin-binding sites on actin?
cards.body:
Troponin (the troponin complex)

The $\ce{Ca^2+}$ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum after an action potential spreads down the T tubules. When $\ce{Ca^2+}$ is pumped back into the SR, tropomyosin blocks the sites again and the muscle relaxes.

Watch out: $\ce{Ca^2+}$ binds **troponin**, not tropomyosin or myosin.
cards.searchQuery: troponin calcium tropomyosin skeletal muscle contraction

cards.title: In the cross-bridge cycle, what must bind to a myosin head to make it let go of actin?
cards.body:
ATP

ATP binding releases the head. Hydrolyzing it to ADP and phosphate then cocks the head into its high-energy position, ready to bind actin and pull again (the **power stroke**).

Example: after death there is no ATP, so myosin stays locked to actin. This is rigor mortis.

Watch out: the filaments slide past each other; neither one shortens.
cards.searchQuery: ATP myosin head detaches actin cross-bridge cycle

cards.title: Trace blood through the heart from the venae cavae to the aorta, naming each chamber and valve in order.
cards.body:
Venae cavae → right atrium → tricuspid valve → right ventricle → pulmonary valve → pulmonary arteries → lungs → pulmonary veins → left atrium → mitral (bicuspid) valve → left ventricle → aortic valve → aorta.

The right side pumps blood to the lungs (**pulmonary circuit**); the left side pumps it to the body (**systemic circuit**).

Watch out: pulmonary arteries carry $\ce{O2}$-poor blood. Arteries carry blood away from the heart, whatever its $\ce{O2}$ content.
cards.searchQuery: path of blood flow through the heart chambers valves

cards.title: What cluster of specialized cells in the wall of the right atrium sets the heart's rhythm as its pacemaker?
cards.body:
The SA (sinoatrial) node

Its impulses spread across both atria through gap junctions. They are delayed about $0.1\,\mathrm{s}$ at the AV node so the atria can empty first, then travel along the bundle branches and Purkinje fibers through the ventricles.

Key idea: the **SA node** is the pacemaker because it fires fastest, so it sets the rate for the whole heart.
cards.searchQuery: SA node sinoatrial pacemaker heart rhythm

cards.title: Trace filtrate through a nephron, from where it forms to the collecting duct.
cards.body:
Bowman's capsule → proximal tubule → loop of Henle → distal tubule → collecting duct.

Blood pressure forces water and small solutes (salts, glucose, amino acids, urea) out of the glomerulus into **Bowman's capsule**. Blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood.

Why: in the loop of Henle, water leaves the descending limb and $\ce{NaCl}$ leaves the ascending limb. This builds the salty medulla that lets the collecting duct concentrate urine.
cards.searchQuery: nephron filtrate path Bowman's capsule loop of Henle collecting duct

cards.title: Which hormone, released from the posterior pituitary when blood osmolarity rises, adds aquaporins to collecting duct cells?
cards.body:
ADH (antidiuretic hormone, also called vasopressin)

ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released by the posterior pituitary. More aquaporins let the kidney reabsorb more water, which concentrates the urine and brings blood osmolarity back down (negative feedback).

Example: alcohol inhibits ADH release, so it produces dilute urine and more of it.
cards.searchQuery: ADH vasopressin aquaporins collecting duct water reabsorption

cards.title: Which adrenal hormone, triggered by the renin–angiotensin system, makes the distal tubule and collecting duct reabsorb more $\ce{Na+}$?
cards.body:
Aldosterone, from the adrenal cortex

Low blood pressure or volume makes the juxtaglomerular apparatus release **renin**, which leads to angiotensin II, and angiotensin II stimulates the adrenal cortex. Reabsorbing more $\ce{Na+}$ (with water following) raises blood volume and pressure.

Watch out: ADH mainly controls water alone; aldosterone controls $\ce{Na+}$ (and water follows).
cards.searchQuery: aldosterone renin angiotensin sodium reabsorption kidney

cards.title: When blood glucose falls between meals, which hormone from pancreatic alpha cells raises it back toward its set point?
cards.body:
Glucagon

Glucagon signals the liver to break down glycogen and release glucose. After a meal, beta cells release **insulin**, which helps body cells take up glucose and the liver store it as glycogen.

Key idea: each hormone's effect reverses the change that triggered it. This is negative feedback.
cards.searchQuery: glucagon alpha cells raise blood glucose liver glycogen

cards.title: Lower pH from $\ce{CO2}$ in active tissues reduces hemoglobin's affinity for $\ce{O2}$, so it unloads more $\ce{O2}$. What is this called?
cards.body:
The Bohr effect (Bohr shift)

The $\ce{O2}$ dissociation curve shifts right. $\ce{CO2}$ reacts with water to form carbonic acid, and the released $\ce{H+}$ binds hemoglobin and changes its shape.

Why: each hemoglobin has 4 subunits, each with an iron-containing heme that binds one $\ce{O2}$. Binding is cooperative, which gives an S-shaped curve.
cards.searchQuery: Bohr effect hemoglobin oxygen dissociation curve pH

cards.title: How does innate immunity differ from adaptive immunity in speed, specificity and memory?
cards.body:
Innate: fast, broad, no memory. Adaptive: slower at first, highly specific, with memory.

**Innate** immunity recognizes molecules shared by broad groups of pathogens (for example through Toll-like receptors). It includes barriers, phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages), natural killer cells and inflammation, and is found in all animals.

**Adaptive** immunity uses highly specific B- and T-cell receptors and builds immunological memory. It is found only in vertebrates.

Tip: think "innate = born with it, same response every time".
cards.searchQuery: innate versus adaptive immunity speed specificity memory

cards.title: What does each do: B cells, helper T cells (CD4) and cytotoxic T cells (CD8)?
cards.body:
B cells make antibodies, helper T cells coordinate, cytotoxic T cells kill infected cells.

- **B cells** become plasma cells that secrete antibodies (humoral response).
- **Helper T (CD4)** cells recognize antigen on class II MHC of antigen-presenting cells, then release cytokines that activate B cells and cytotoxic T cells.
- **Cytotoxic T (CD8)** cells recognize antigen on class I MHC and kill infected or cancer cells with perforin and granzymes.

Example: HIV destroys helper T cells, which cripples both arms of adaptive immunity.
cards.searchQuery: B cells helper T cells cytotoxic T cells roles immune response

cards.title: Why do steroid hormones bind receptors inside target cells, while peptide hormones like insulin bind receptors on the surface?
cards.body:
Steroids are lipid-soluble and cross the membrane; peptides are water-soluble and cannot.

**Steroids** (for example cortisol and estradiol) diffuse through the plasma membrane and bind intracellular receptors. The hormone–receptor complex then acts as a transcription factor.

**Peptide hormones** can't cross the membrane, so they bind surface receptors that trigger signal transduction, often through second messengers like cAMP.

Key idea: solubility decides where the receptor is.
cards.searchQuery: steroid versus peptide hormones receptor location lipid soluble

cards.title: What term describes the maintenance of a relatively stable internal environment despite changes outside?
cards.body:
Homeostasis

Homeostasis keeps variables such as body temperature, blood pH, blood glucose and water balance within a narrow range. Most of it works by feedback loops with a sensor, a control center and an effector.

Example: if body temperature rises, the hypothalamus triggers sweating and skin vasodilation, which cools the body.

Watch out: stable does not mean constant. Variables fluctuate around a **set point**.
cards.searchQuery: homeostasis definition stable internal environment set point

cards.title: What type of feedback reverses a change and keeps a variable near its set point?
cards.body:
Negative feedback

The response opposes the stimulus, so the change shrinks. Most homeostatic controls work this way.

Example: rising blood glucose triggers insulin release, which lowers glucose; falling glucose triggers glucagon, which raises it.

Watch out: "negative" means the response opposes the change. It does not mean the effect is bad.
cards.searchQuery: negative feedback homeostasis set point example

cards.title: What type of feedback amplifies a change, as when oxytocin strengthens uterine contractions during childbirth?
cards.body:
Positive feedback

The response pushes the variable further in the same direction, until something outside the loop stops it.

Example: contractions push the baby's head against the cervix, which triggers more oxytocin, which causes stronger contractions, until birth.

Key idea: **positive feedback** drives a process to completion; **negative feedback** stabilizes.
cards.searchQuery: positive feedback oxytocin childbirth contractions

cards.title: What term describes animals, such as birds and mammals, that generate most of their body heat through their own metabolism?
cards.body:
Endotherms

Endotherms keep a high, fairly constant body temperature but pay for it with a high energy cost (high metabolic rate).

Why: **ectotherms** such as reptiles and amphibians gain most of their heat from the environment, so they need far less food per unit mass.

Watch out: "warm-blooded" and "cold-blooded" are informal. Some ectotherms keep a steady temperature by behavior, such as basking.
cards.searchQuery: endotherm versus ectotherm body heat metabolism

cards.title: Which long extension of a neuron conducts action potentials away from the cell body?
cards.body:
The axon

An axon ends in branches called axon terminals, which release neurotransmitter onto the next cell. **Dendrites**, in contrast, are the shorter, branched extensions that receive incoming signals.

Key idea: signals flow dendrites → cell body → axon → axon terminals.
cards.searchQuery: neuron axon carries action potential away from cell body

cards.title: What roles do sensory neurons, interneurons and motor neurons play in the nervous system?
cards.body:
Sensory neurons carry information in, interneurons integrate it, motor neurons carry commands out.

- **Sensory neurons** carry information from receptors toward the CNS.
- **Interneurons** are located within the CNS and integrate information.
- **Motor neurons** carry commands from the CNS to effectors such as muscles and glands.

Tip: most neurons in the human brain are interneurons.
cards.searchQuery: sensory neurons interneurons motor neurons functions

cards.title: An action potential's size does not depend on how strong the stimulus was, as long as threshold is reached. What principle is this?
cards.body:
The all-or-none principle

Once threshold is reached, the action potential always has the same size. A stronger stimulus does not make it larger.

Why: the neuron signals a stronger stimulus by firing action potentials more often (higher frequency), and by recruiting more neurons.

Watch out: the **graded potentials** at dendrites do vary in size; only action potentials are all-or-none.
cards.searchQuery: all-or-none principle action potential stimulus strength frequency

cards.title: How do an excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) and an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) differ?
cards.body:
An EPSP depolarizes the postsynaptic cell; an IPSP hyperpolarizes it.

An **EPSP** moves the membrane potential toward threshold, for example when $\ce{Na+}$ channels open. An **IPSP** moves it away from threshold, for example when $\ce{K+}$ channels or $\ce{Cl-}$ channels open.

Why: a neuron adds up all the EPSPs and IPSPs it receives. It fires an action potential only if the total reaches threshold at the axon hillock.

Key idea: it is the receptor and channel type, not the neurotransmitter alone, that decides whether a synapse excites or inhibits.
cards.searchQuery: EPSP IPSP excitatory inhibitory postsynaptic potential difference

cards.title: Which neurotransmitter do motor neurons release at the neuromuscular junction to make a skeletal muscle fiber contract?
cards.body:
Acetylcholine (ACh)

ACh binds receptors on the muscle fiber membrane. This opens ligand-gated channels, depolarizes the fiber and starts an action potential that spreads down the T tubules.

Example: botulinum toxin blocks ACh release, causing paralysis.
cards.searchQuery: acetylcholine neuromuscular junction motor neuron neurotransmitter

cards.title: Which enzyme in the synaptic cleft breaks down acetylcholine and so ends the signal?
cards.body:
Acetylcholinesterase (AChE)

The enzyme splits acetylcholine, so each signal at the synapse is brief and the muscle can relax.

Example: nerve agents and some pesticides inhibit **acetylcholinesterase**, so ACh builds up and muscles contract continuously.
cards.searchQuery: acetylcholinesterase breaks down acetylcholine synaptic cleft

cards.title: Which division of the autonomic nervous system speeds the heart and prepares the body for "fight or flight"?
cards.body:
The sympathetic division

It raises heart rate, dilates the bronchioles, releases glucose from the liver and slows digestion.

Key idea: sympathetic = **fight or flight**; its main chemical messengers are norepinephrine and epinephrine.

Tip: think "S" for "stress".
cards.searchQuery: sympathetic nervous system fight or flight heart rate

cards.title: Which division of the autonomic nervous system slows the heart and promotes digestion, the "rest and digest" state?
cards.body:
The parasympathetic division

It lowers heart rate, constricts the bronchioles and stimulates the digestive organs.

Key idea: parasympathetic = **rest and digest**, the opposite of the sympathetic division. Most organs receive input from both.

Example: the vagus nerve carries much of the parasympathetic signal to the heart and gut.
cards.searchQuery: parasympathetic nervous system rest and digest heart rate

cards.title: What are the five components of a reflex arc, in order?
cards.body:
Receptor → sensory neuron → integration center (CNS) → motor neuron → effector.

The integration center is usually the spinal cord, so the response occurs before the brain is aware of the stimulus.

Example: in the knee-jerk reflex, a stretch receptor in the thigh muscle signals the spinal cord, and a motor neuron makes that same muscle contract.

Watch out: some simple reflexes, such as the knee-jerk, use a direct sensory-to-motor synapse with no interneuron.
cards.searchQuery: reflex arc components receptor sensory neuron effector spinal cord

cards.title: Which part of the brain coordinates balance and fine-tunes voluntary movement?
cards.body:
The cerebellum

It compares intended movements with sensory feedback from muscles and joints and corrects them, which smooths and coordinates motion.

Example: damage to the **cerebellum** causes clumsy, uncoordinated movement, though muscles are not paralyzed.
cards.searchQuery: cerebellum function balance coordination movement

cards.title: Which part of the brainstem controls automatic functions such as breathing rate and heart rate?
cards.body:
The medulla oblongata

It contains centers for breathing, heart rate and blood pressure, and also for reflexes such as swallowing, coughing and vomiting.

Why: the medulla senses blood $\ce{CO2}$ and pH and adjusts the breathing rate, and this happens without conscious effort.
cards.searchQuery: medulla oblongata brainstem breathing heart rate control

cards.title: Which brain region links the nervous and endocrine systems and acts as the body's thermostat?
cards.body:
The hypothalamus

It monitors body temperature, hunger, thirst and daily rhythms, and it controls the pituitary gland. It makes ADH and oxytocin (released by the posterior pituitary) and releasing hormones that act on the anterior pituitary.

Key idea: the **hypothalamus** is the main control center for homeostasis in the brain.
cards.searchQuery: hypothalamus function thermostat pituitary homeostasis

cards.title: What type of sensory receptor responds to touch, pressure, stretch and sound vibrations?
cards.body:
Mechanoreceptors

They respond to mechanical deformation, which opens ion channels in the receptor cell.

Example: touch receptors in the skin, stretch receptors in muscle and the hair cells of the inner ear are all **mechanoreceptors**.

Tip: compare chemoreceptors (taste, smell, blood chemistry), thermoreceptors (temperature) and photoreceptors (light).
cards.searchQuery: mechanoreceptors touch pressure stretch sensory receptor types

cards.title: What is the repeating contractile unit of a skeletal muscle myofibril, running from one Z line to the next?
cards.body:
The sarcomere

A myofibril is a chain of sarcomeres end to end. Each one contains overlapping thin (actin) and thick (myosin) filaments.

Key idea: when a muscle contracts, every **sarcomere** shortens, so the whole fiber shortens.
cards.searchQuery: sarcomere contractile unit myofibril Z line

cards.title: In a sarcomere, which protein makes up the thick filaments and which makes up the thin filaments?
cards.body:
Thick filaments are myosin; thin filaments are actin.

The thin filaments are anchored at the Z lines and also carry **tropomyosin** and **troponin**. The myosin heads on the thick filaments reach out and bind actin to pull.

Mnemonic: **myosin** is the **m**otor, and it is the **thick** one.
cards.searchQuery: thick filaments myosin thin filaments actin sarcomere

cards.title: During contraction of a skeletal muscle fiber, which band of the sarcomere stays the same length?
cards.body:
The A band

The A band is the full length of the thick filaments, and they don't shorten. The I band (thin filaments only) and the H zone (thick filaments only) get shorter as the filaments overlap more.

Why: this is the evidence for the **sliding filament model**: the filaments slide past each other and neither shortens.
cards.searchQuery: sliding filament A band I band H zone sarcomere shortening

cards.title: Which muscle type is striated, has one nucleus per cell, is connected by intercalated discs and contracts involuntarily?
cards.body:
Cardiac muscle

The **intercalated discs** contain gap junctions that let the action potential spread from cell to cell, so the heart contracts as a unit.

Watch out: skeletal muscle is striated but voluntary and multinucleate; smooth muscle is involuntary but not striated.
cards.searchQuery: cardiac muscle intercalated discs striated involuntary

cards.title: Which muscle type lines the walls of the intestines and blood vessels, lacks striations and contracts involuntarily?
cards.body:
Smooth muscle

Its filaments are not lined up in sarcomeres, so it looks smooth. It contracts slowly and can stay contracted for long periods without tiring.

Example: waves of **smooth muscle** contraction (peristalsis) move food through the gut, and contraction of vessel walls changes blood pressure.
cards.searchQuery: smooth muscle involuntary non-striated walls of organs

cards.title: How do slow-twitch (type I) and fast-twitch (type II) skeletal muscle fibers differ?
cards.body:
Slow-twitch fibers resist fatigue; fast-twitch fibers contract faster and fatigue sooner.

- **Slow-twitch:** rely on aerobic respiration, have many mitochondria, capillaries and myoglobin (red), and suit endurance such as distance running.
- **Fast-twitch:** generate force quickly and rely more on glycolysis, and tire quickly. They suit sprints and lifting.

Example: postural muscles are rich in slow-twitch fibers.
cards.searchQuery: slow-twitch versus fast-twitch muscle fibers type I type II

cards.title: Which molecule stored in muscle quickly regenerates ATP by passing a phosphate group to ADP during the first seconds of intense exercise?
cards.body:
Creatine phosphate (phosphocreatine)

It supplies ATP almost instantly but only lasts about ten seconds of maximal effort. After that, muscle relies on glycolysis and then on aerobic respiration.

Why: muscle stores only a small amount of ATP, so it needs a **rapid backup** system.
cards.searchQuery: creatine phosphate regenerates ATP muscle first seconds exercise

cards.title: Why do arteries have thicker, more elastic walls than veins?
cards.body:
Arteries carry blood at much higher pressure.

The thick walls withstand the pressure surge from each heartbeat, and their **elastic** recoil keeps blood moving between beats.

Why: veins carry blood at low pressure back to the heart, so they have thinner walls and one-way valves instead.
cards.searchQuery: artery versus vein wall structure elastic thickness pressure

cards.title: Which vessels, with walls only one cell thick, are the sites of exchange of gases, nutrients and wastes with the tissues?
cards.body:
Capillaries

The thin walls and large total surface area let substances diffuse quickly. Blood slows in the capillary beds because their combined cross-section is huge, which gives more time for exchange.

Watch out: capillaries connect arterioles to venules; arteries and veins don't exchange materials with tissue.
cards.searchQuery: capillaries exchange gases nutrients thin walls

cards.title: What structures in veins prevent blood from flowing backward, with help from the squeezing of nearby skeletal muscles?
cards.body:
Valves (one-way valves)

Blood in veins is at low pressure, so contraction of nearby skeletal muscles squeezes it forward, and the **valves** stop it from falling back.

Example: standing still for a long time lets blood pool in the legs, because the muscle pump isn't working.
cards.searchQuery: vein valves prevent backflow skeletal muscle pump

cards.title: What is the term for the phase of the cardiac cycle in which the ventricles contract and eject blood?
cards.body:
Systole (ventricular systole)

Blood is forced out into the aorta and pulmonary artery. **Diastole** is the relaxation phase, when the chambers fill with blood.

Tip: systole = squeeze.
cards.searchQuery: systole ventricular contraction cardiac cycle diastole

cards.title: In a blood pressure reading of $120/80\,\mathrm{mm\,Hg}$, what do the two numbers represent?
cards.body:
$120$ is the systolic pressure; $80$ is the diastolic pressure.

**Systolic** pressure is the peak pressure in the arteries while the ventricles contract. **Diastolic** pressure is the lowest pressure, while the ventricles relax and fill.

Watch out: the units are millimeters of mercury, and the pressure is measured in the arteries, not in the heart chambers.
cards.searchQuery: blood pressure reading systolic diastolic 120 over 80

cards.title: What causes the "lub-dub" sounds of a heartbeat?
cards.body:
The closing of the heart valves.

- "Lub": the atrioventricular (tricuspid and mitral) valves close as the ventricles begin to contract.
- "Dub": the semilunar (aortic and pulmonary) valves close as the ventricles relax.

Example: a heart murmur is often the sound of blood leaking back or flowing turbulently through a faulty valve.
cards.searchQuery: lub dub heart sounds valves closing AV semilunar

cards.title: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by what other quantity?
cards.body:
Stroke volume

Stroke volume is the volume of blood pumped by one ventricle in a single beat.

Example: at rest, $70\,\mathrm{beats/min} \times 70\,\mathrm{mL/beat} = 4900\,\mathrm{mL/min}$, so about $5\,\mathrm{L/min}$.

Key idea: exercise raises **cardiac output** by raising both heart rate and stroke volume.
cards.searchQuery: cardiac output heart rate stroke volume formula

cards.title: How many times does blood pass through the heart in one complete circuit of the body in a fish, and in a mammal?
cards.body:
Fish: once. Mammal: twice.

In a fish, blood goes heart → gills → body → heart (single circulation), so the pressure drops after the gills. A mammal has **double circulation**, with a pulmonary circuit and a systemic circuit, and the heart boosts the pressure again between them.

Why: double circulation delivers blood to the body at high pressure.
cards.searchQuery: single versus double circulation fish mammal heart

cards.title: What fluid component makes up about 55% of the volume of blood?
cards.body:
Plasma

Plasma is mostly water and carries dissolved ions, nutrients, hormones, wastes and proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen.

Key idea: the remaining 45% or so is the cells: mostly red blood cells, plus white blood cells and platelets.
cards.searchQuery: blood plasma composition percentage of blood volume

cards.title: Which cell fragments in blood plug a damaged vessel and help start clotting?
cards.body:
Platelets (thrombocytes)

Platelets stick to the damaged wall and release chemicals that trigger the clotting cascade. This converts the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen into insoluble **fibrin** threads that form a mesh.

Watch out: platelets are fragments of larger cells, not whole cells.
cards.searchQuery: platelets clotting fibrin fibrinogen blood clot

cards.title: At the arterial end of a capillary bed, why does fluid tend to leave the capillary, and why does it return at the venous end?
cards.body:
Arterial end: blood pressure is higher than the osmotic pull of the blood proteins. Venous end: the osmotic pull wins.

Blood pressure (hydrostatic) pushes fluid out, and the osmotic pressure from plasma proteins pulls it back in. Pressure drops along the capillary, so the balance flips.

Why: not all the fluid returns. The excess is picked up by the **lymphatic system**.
cards.searchQuery: capillary fluid exchange blood pressure osmotic pressure arterial venous end

cards.title: Which tiny air sacs in the lungs are the site of gas exchange with the blood?
cards.body:
Alveoli

Each alveolus has a wall one cell thick, wrapped in capillaries. $\ce{O2}$ diffuses into the blood and $\ce{CO2}$ diffuses out. Together they give a huge surface area, around the size of a tennis court.

Why: a thin, moist, large surface is what makes **diffusion** fast.
cards.searchQuery: alveoli gas exchange lungs thin walls capillaries

cards.title: How does contraction of the diaphragm cause air to flow into the lungs?
cards.body:
It enlarges the chest cavity, so the pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure.

The diaphragm flattens and the rib muscles lift the ribs, so thoracic volume increases and pressure drops (**negative-pressure breathing**). Air then flows in from high to low pressure.

Key idea: mammals pull air in; they do not push it in. Exhalation at rest is passive, as the diaphragm relaxes and the lungs recoil.
cards.searchQuery: inhalation diaphragm contracts negative pressure breathing lungs

cards.title: Respiratory gases diffuse from a region of higher to lower what?
cards.body:
Partial pressure

The partial pressure of a gas is its share of the total pressure. Each gas diffuses independently down its own gradient.

Example: in the alveoli $P_{\ce{O2}}$ is higher than in arriving blood, so $\ce{O2}$ enters the blood. In the tissues $P_{\ce{O2}}$ is lower than in the blood, so $\ce{O2}$ leaves it.

Watch out: $\ce{CO2}$ moves the other way, from tissue to blood to alveoli, because its partial pressure is highest in the tissues.
cards.searchQuery: partial pressure gradient gas exchange diffusion oxygen carbon dioxide

cards.title: In what chemical form is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
cards.body:
Bicarbonate ($\ce{HCO3-}$)

About 70% of the $\ce{CO2}$ is carried this way. In red blood cells, $\ce{CO2}$ reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which dissociates:

$$\ce{CO2 + H2O <=> H2CO3 <=> H+ + HCO3-}$$

The rest is bound to hemoglobin or dissolved in plasma. In the lungs the reaction runs in reverse, and the $\ce{CO2}$ is exhaled.
cards.searchQuery: carbon dioxide transport blood bicarbonate ion

cards.title: Which enzyme in red blood cells speeds up the reaction of $\ce{CO2}$ with water to form carbonic acid?
cards.body:
Carbonic anhydrase

The enzyme makes the reaction fast enough that $\ce{CO2}$ can be converted to bicarbonate as blood passes through the tissue capillaries.

Why: the $\ce{H+}$ released is buffered by hemoglobin, which also promotes the **Bohr effect**.
cards.searchQuery: carbonic anhydrase red blood cells CO2 carbonic acid

cards.title: Which change in the blood is the main stimulus that makes the brain increase the breathing rate?
cards.body:
A rise in $\ce{CO2}$ (which lowers pH).

Chemoreceptors in the medulla sense the pH change, and the medulla increases the breathing rate to exhale more $\ce{CO2}$.

Watch out: falling $\ce{O2}$ also stimulates breathing, through sensors in the carotid and aortic bodies, but only when it drops quite low.
cards.searchQuery: breathing rate control carbon dioxide pH medulla chemoreceptors

cards.title: In fish gills, why does water flow past the gill filaments in the opposite direction to the blood?
cards.body:
It keeps a diffusion gradient for $\ce{O2}$ along the whole length of the gill.

The blood is always meeting water with a higher $\ce{O2}$ content than itself, so $\ce{O2}$ keeps diffusing in. This **countercurrent exchange** lets the fish extract a large fraction of the dissolved $\ce{O2}$.

Why: with parallel flow, the two would equalize halfway along and exchange would stop.
cards.searchQuery: countercurrent exchange fish gills oxygen diffusion gradient

cards.title: Why must fetal hemoglobin have a higher affinity for $\ce{O2}$ than adult hemoglobin?
cards.body:
So the fetus can take $\ce{O2}$ from the mother's blood in the placenta.

At the same $P_{\ce{O2}}$, fetal hemoglobin holds $\ce{O2}$ more tightly, so $\ce{O2}$ passes from maternal hemoglobin to fetal hemoglobin.

Key idea: its **dissociation curve** lies to the left of the adult curve.
cards.searchQuery: fetal hemoglobin higher oxygen affinity placenta dissociation curve

cards.title: Which enzyme in saliva begins the chemical digestion of starch in the mouth?
cards.body:
Salivary amylase

Amylase breaks starch into smaller sugars, such as maltose. It stops working in the acid of the stomach.

Example: chew a cracker for a while and it starts to taste sweet, as starch is turned into sugar.
cards.searchQuery: salivary amylase starch digestion mouth

cards.title: Which stomach enzyme digests proteins and works best in the strongly acidic gastric juice?
cards.body:
Pepsin

Pepsin is released in an inactive form, **pepsinogen**, and is activated by stomach acid ($\ce{HCl}$). It cuts proteins into shorter polypeptides. Its optimum is at about pH $2$.

Why: secreting an inactive precursor stops the enzyme digesting the cells that make it.
cards.searchQuery: pepsin pepsinogen stomach protein digestion pH 2

cards.title: What two roles does hydrochloric acid play in the stomach?
cards.body:
It activates pepsin, and it kills or denatures much of what you swallow.

- It converts pepsinogen into active **pepsin** and provides the low pH pepsin needs.
- It denatures proteins and kills many microbes in food.

Watch out: acid does not digest the proteins itself. The enzyme pepsin does that.
cards.searchQuery: hydrochloric acid stomach functions activate pepsin kill microbes

cards.title: Which first segment of the small intestine receives chyme from the stomach, bile from the liver and enzymes from the pancreas?
cards.body:
The duodenum

Most chemical digestion happens here. Bile and pancreatic juice enter through a duct, and the pancreatic juice's bicarbonate neutralizes the acidic chyme.

Key idea: most nutrient absorption then occurs further along, in the jejunum and ileum.
cards.searchQuery: duodenum small intestine chyme bile pancreatic juice digestion

cards.title: Which finger-like projections of the small intestine lining, themselves covered in microvilli, increase its absorptive surface area?
cards.body:
Villi

Each villus contains capillaries and a lymph vessel (lacteal) to carry absorbed nutrients away. The microvilli on its cells further increase the area.

Key idea: a large surface area means faster absorption, the same principle as in the alveoli.
cards.searchQuery: intestinal villi microvilli surface area absorption small intestine

cards.title: Which fluid, made in the liver and stored in the gallbladder, helps break fat into small droplets so lipase can digest it?
cards.body:
Bile

Bile salts **emulsify** fat, breaking large globules into tiny droplets and increasing the surface area for lipase to work on.

Watch out: bile is not an enzyme and does not chemically digest fat. It only emulsifies.
cards.searchQuery: bile emulsifies fat liver gallbladder lipase

cards.title: Which organ releases digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases) and bicarbonate into the duodenum?
cards.body:
The pancreas

Its enzymes digest carbohydrates, fats and proteins, and the **bicarbonate** neutralizes stomach acid so the enzymes can work.

Key idea: the pancreas is both an exocrine gland (digestive enzymes, through a duct) and an endocrine gland (insulin and glucagon, into blood).
cards.searchQuery: pancreas digestive enzymes bicarbonate duodenum exocrine

cards.title: Into which lymph vessels within each intestinal villus do most absorbed fats pass?
cards.body:
Lacteals

Absorbed fatty acids are reassembled into triglycerides inside the intestinal cells and packaged with protein into chylomicrons, which are too large to enter capillaries. They enter the **lacteals** and travel in the lymph before reaching the blood.

Why: sugars and amino acids, in contrast, go directly into the villus capillaries.
cards.searchQuery: lacteals fat absorption chylomicrons villus lymph

cards.title: Which vessel carries blood rich in absorbed sugars and amino acids from the intestines to the liver?
cards.body:
The hepatic portal vein

The liver processes the nutrients before they reach the rest of the body, for example by storing glucose as glycogen and removing toxins.

Key idea: this is a **portal system**: a vein that runs between two capillary beds, the intestines and the liver.
cards.searchQuery: hepatic portal vein intestine liver nutrients

cards.title: What is the main function of the large intestine?
cards.body:
It reabsorbs water, and compacts the remaining waste into feces.

Its bacteria (the gut microbiome) ferment some undigested material and make vitamins such as vitamin K.

Watch out: diarrhea means the water was not reabsorbed; constipation means too much was.
cards.searchQuery: large intestine function water reabsorption feces

cards.title: Which process forces water and small solutes out of the glomerulus into Bowman's capsule?
cards.body:
Filtration (glomerular filtration, or ultrafiltration)

Blood pressure in the glomerulus drives it. Water, salts, glucose, amino acids and urea pass through, while blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood.

Watch out: this step is not selective. The body's selection happens later, by **reabsorption** in the tubule.
cards.searchQuery: glomerular filtration Bowman's capsule blood pressure nephron

cards.title: In which part of the nephron is nearly all of the filtered glucose and amino acids reabsorbed?
cards.body:
The proximal tubule

The proximal tubule also reabsorbs about two-thirds of the filtered $\ce{NaCl}$ and water. Glucose and amino acids are taken up by transport proteins, and in healthy people none is left in the urine.

Example: in untreated diabetes, glucose in the filtrate exceeds what the transporters can carry, so glucose appears in urine.
cards.searchQuery: proximal tubule reabsorption glucose amino acids nephron

cards.title: What is tubular secretion in the kidney?
cards.body:
The movement of substances from the blood into the filtrate in the tubule.

It adds substances that were not filtered, or that need extra removal, such as $\ce{H+}$, $\ce{K+}$ and many drugs.

Key idea: **reabsorption** moves substances filtrate → blood; **secretion** moves them blood → filtrate.
cards.searchQuery: tubular secretion kidney blood to filtrate versus reabsorption

cards.title: Which nitrogenous waste do mammals make in the liver from ammonia and excrete in urine?
cards.body:
Urea

Ammonia from the breakdown of amino acids is very toxic, so the liver converts it to **urea**, which is far less toxic and can be carried in the blood to the kidneys.

Watch out: urea is made in the liver, not in the kidney; the kidney only excretes it.
cards.searchQuery: urea nitrogenous waste liver ammonia mammals

cards.title: How do ammonia, urea and uric acid compare as nitrogenous wastes in toxicity, water needed and energy cost to make?
cards.body:
Ammonia: most toxic, needs the most water, cheapest to make. Uric acid: least toxic, needs the least water, costs the most energy. Urea is in between.

- **Ammonia:** excreted by most aquatic animals, such as fishes, which have plenty of water to dilute it.
- **Urea:** mammals and most adult amphibians.
- **Uric acid:** birds, insects and many reptiles, excreted as a semisolid paste that saves water.

Example: uric acid suits egg-laying animals, because the waste can be stored safely inside the egg.
cards.searchQuery: ammonia urea uric acid nitrogenous waste comparison water energy

cards.title: How do endocrine glands deliver their products differently from exocrine glands?
cards.body:
Endocrine glands release hormones into the blood; exocrine glands release secretions through ducts.

Hormones travel in the bloodstream and act only on cells with the matching receptor. Exocrine secretions, such as sweat, saliva and digestive enzymes, go onto a surface or into a cavity.

Example: the pancreas is both: it secretes digestive enzymes through a duct and insulin directly into the blood.
cards.searchQuery: endocrine versus exocrine glands hormones ducts blood

cards.title: Which gland, controlled by the hypothalamus, is often called the "master gland" because many of its hormones regulate other glands?
cards.body:
The pituitary gland

The **anterior pituitary** makes hormones such as TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH and growth hormone. The **posterior pituitary** stores and releases ADH and oxytocin, which are made in the hypothalamus.

Key idea: the hypothalamus controls the pituitary, and the pituitary controls many other endocrine glands.
cards.searchQuery: pituitary master gland anterior posterior hormones hypothalamus

cards.title: Which hormone from the thyroid gland raises the body's metabolic rate? (Give its common name, or abbreviation T4.)
cards.body:
Thyroxine (T4)

Thyroxine (T4) and the related T3 raise metabolic rate and are needed for normal growth and development. The pituitary hormone **TSH** stimulates their release, and high T4 feeds back to lower TSH (negative feedback).

Example: too little thyroid hormone (hypothyroidism) causes weight gain, fatigue and feeling cold.
cards.searchQuery: thyroxine T4 thyroid hormone metabolic rate TSH

cards.title: Which mineral is needed to make thyroid hormone, so that a shortage can cause an enlarged thyroid (goiter)?
cards.body:
Iodine

Without iodine the thyroid can't make T3 and T4, so negative feedback fails and the pituitary keeps releasing TSH. TSH keeps stimulating the thyroid, which enlarges.

Example: **goiter** was once common inland, until iodized salt became widespread.
cards.searchQuery: iodine deficiency goiter thyroid hormone TSH

cards.title: Which hormone from the parathyroid glands raises blood calcium when it is too low?
cards.body:
Parathyroid hormone (PTH)

PTH stimulates the release of $\ce{Ca^2+}$ from bone, increases its reabsorption in the kidney and increases its absorption from the gut (by activating vitamin D).

Key idea: **calcitonin**, from the thyroid, lowers blood $\ce{Ca^2+}$. They are a pair of opposing hormones.
cards.searchQuery: parathyroid hormone PTH raises blood calcium bone calcitonin

cards.title: Which hormone from the adrenal medulla triggers the fight-or-flight response?
cards.body:
Epinephrine (adrenaline)

It raises heart rate and blood glucose, and diverts blood to skeletal muscle. It works quickly because it is released with the sympathetic nervous system.

Watch out: the adrenal **medulla** (inner) makes epinephrine; the adrenal **cortex** (outer) makes steroids such as cortisol and aldosterone.
cards.searchQuery: epinephrine adrenaline adrenal medulla fight or flight

cards.title: Which steroid hormone from the adrenal cortex is released during long-term stress and raises blood glucose?
cards.body:
Cortisol

Cortisol promotes glucose production in the liver and the breakdown of protein and fat. It also suppresses inflammation and the immune system.

Watch out: long-term high cortisol weakens immunity, which is why chronic stress can leave you more prone to infection.
cards.searchQuery: cortisol adrenal cortex long-term stress blood glucose

cards.title: How does type 1 diabetes differ from type 2 diabetes in its cause?
cards.body:
Type 1: the body makes too little insulin. Type 2: target cells respond poorly to insulin.

- **Type 1** is an autoimmune attack that destroys the pancreatic beta cells, so little or no insulin is made.
- **Type 2** is mainly insulin resistance, where target cells respond poorly to insulin. It is linked to obesity and inactivity.

Example: in both, blood glucose stays high after meals and glucose can spill into the urine.
cards.searchQuery: type 1 versus type 2 diabetes insulin beta cells resistance

cards.title: Which hormone from the posterior pituitary stimulates uterine contractions during labor and milk ejection during nursing?
cards.body:
Oxytocin

Oxytocin is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary. In labor it is part of a positive feedback loop. In nursing, the infant's suckling triggers its release.

Example: doctors may give synthetic oxytocin to induce labor.
cards.searchQuery: oxytocin posterior pituitary uterine contractions milk ejection

cards.title: What general name is given to white blood cells such as neutrophils and macrophages that engulf and digest pathogens?
cards.body:
Phagocytes

They engulf microbes by **phagocytosis** and destroy them in lysosomes. They are part of the innate defense and respond within minutes to hours.

Example: macrophages also display pieces of what they digested to helper T cells, linking innate to adaptive immunity.
cards.searchQuery: phagocytes neutrophils macrophages phagocytosis innate immunity

cards.title: How many polypeptide chains make up a basic antibody (immunoglobulin) molecule?
cards.body:
4

Two identical heavy chains and two identical light chains form a Y shape. The tips of the Y have two identical antigen-binding sites.

Key idea: the variable regions at the tips decide which antigen the **antibody** recognizes.
cards.searchQuery: antibody structure four polypeptide chains heavy light

cards.title: What process describes how an antigen selects the lymphocytes whose receptors fit it, which then multiply into a clone?
cards.body:
Clonal selection

A pathogen's antigen binds only the few B or T cells with a matching receptor. These cells divide to form effector cells (which fight the infection) and **memory cells** (which persist).

Why: each lymphocyte already carries one specific receptor before it ever meets an antigen. The antigen selects; it does not shape the receptor.
cards.searchQuery: clonal selection lymphocytes antigen memory cells effector cells

cards.title: Why is the secondary immune response faster and stronger than the primary response?
cards.body:
Memory cells made during the first exposure respond immediately.

Memory B and T cells are already present and quickly multiply into many effector cells and plasma cells, so the antibody level rises within days and reaches a higher peak.

Key idea: this immunological memory is the basis of **vaccination**.
cards.searchQuery: secondary immune response memory cells faster stronger primary

cards.title: How does a vaccine protect against a later infection?
cards.body:
It exposes the immune system to a harmless form of an antigen, which creates memory cells.

The vaccine may contain a weakened or killed pathogen, a piece of one, or mRNA that tells your cells to make an antigen. The primary response happens without disease, so the real infection triggers a rapid secondary response.

Watch out: most vaccines don't give the antibodies directly. They cause the body to make its own antibodies and memory cells.
cards.searchQuery: how vaccines work memory cells antigen immune response

cards.title: Which chemical released by mast cells during allergic reactions causes swelling, itching and runny nose by widening and leaking blood vessels?
cards.body:
Histamine

In an allergy, IgE antibodies on mast cells bind the allergen, and the mast cells then release **histamine**. It makes capillaries wider and leakier.

Example: antihistamine drugs block histamine receptors and relieve the symptoms.
cards.searchQuery: histamine mast cells allergy inflammation IgE

cards.title: What is an autoimmune disease?
cards.body:
A disease in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissues.

Self-tolerance fails, and lymphocytes treat normal cells as foreign.

Example: in type 1 diabetes it attacks beta cells; in multiple sclerosis it attacks myelin; in rheumatoid arthritis it attacks the joints.
cards.searchQuery: autoimmune disease immune system attacks own tissues examples

cards.title: A newborn gets antibodies from its mother through the placenta and breast milk. Is this active or passive immunity?
cards.body:
Passive immunity

The baby receives ready-made antibodies, so it has no memory cells of its own and the protection fades in weeks to months.

Watch out: active immunity means your own immune system made the antibodies, either after infection or after vaccination.
cards.searchQuery: passive immunity antibodies mother placenta breast milk newborn

cards.title: Which innate lymphocytes kill virus-infected cells and some tumor cells without needing prior exposure?
cards.body:
Natural killer (NK) cells

NK cells release perforin and enzymes that trigger the target cell to die by apoptosis.

Watch out: NK cells are part of **innate** immunity: they act without antigen-specific receptors and make no memory. Cytotoxic T cells do a similar job but are adaptive.
cards.searchQuery: natural killer cells innate immunity virus-infected tumor cells

cards.title: How many functional gametes result from one primary spermatocyte and from one primary oocyte completing meiosis?
cards.body:
Spermatocyte: 4 sperm. Oocyte: 1 egg.

In oogenesis the divisions are unequal, so almost all the cytoplasm goes to one cell, and the other cells are small **polar bodies** that degenerate.

Why: the egg needs the stored nutrients to support early development, while sperm need only be small and mobile.
cards.searchQuery: spermatogenesis versus oogenesis number of gametes polar bodies

cards.title: A surge of which pituitary hormone around the middle of the menstrual cycle triggers ovulation?
cards.body:
LH (luteinizing hormone)

Rising estrogen from the growing follicle causes the LH surge. LH makes the follicle release its egg (ovulation), around day 14 of a 28-day cycle.

Key idea: **FSH** stimulates the follicle to grow; **LH** triggers ovulation and then turns the empty follicle into the corpus luteum.
cards.searchQuery: LH surge ovulation menstrual cycle luteinizing hormone

cards.title: Which structure, formed from the follicle after ovulation, secretes progesterone and some estrogen?
cards.body:
The corpus luteum

Progesterone maintains and thickens the uterine lining. If no embryo implants, the corpus luteum degenerates after about two weeks.

Why: falling progesterone and estrogen levels cause the lining to be shed, which is **menstruation**.
cards.searchQuery: corpus luteum progesterone uterine lining menstrual cycle

cards.title: Which hormone, made by the early embryo, keeps the corpus luteum active and is detected by pregnancy tests?
cards.body:
hCG (human chorionic gonadotropin)

hCG acts like LH, so the corpus luteum keeps making progesterone and the lining is not shed. Later the placenta makes enough progesterone itself.

Key idea: **hCG** is the signal from the embryo that says "pregnant".
cards.searchQuery: hCG human chorionic gonadotropin pregnancy corpus luteum

cards.title: Which cells in the testes, stimulated by LH, produce testosterone?
cards.body:
Leydig cells (interstitial cells)

They lie between the seminiferous tubules, where sperm are made. **Sertoli cells**, inside the tubules, nourish the developing sperm and respond to FSH.

Key idea: LH acts on Leydig cells, and FSH acts on Sertoli cells.
cards.searchQuery: Leydig cells testosterone LH testes Sertoli FSH

cards.title: Which cap-like structure at the tip of a sperm contains enzymes that digest a path through the egg's outer layers?
cards.body:
The acrosome

When the sperm reaches the egg's outer layer, the acrosome releases its enzymes (the acrosomal reaction) so the sperm can reach the egg membrane.

Example: after one sperm fuses with the egg, the egg's outer layers change to block other sperm, which prevents polyspermy.
cards.searchQuery: acrosome sperm enzymes egg outer layer fertilization

cards.title: Which organ allows nutrient, gas and waste exchange between mother and fetus, without mixing their blood?
cards.body:
The placenta

Maternal and fetal blood flow close to each other, separated by thin membranes, and substances diffuse across. It also makes hormones, including progesterone, estrogen and hCG.

Watch out: some substances cross it too, including alcohol, many drugs and some viruses.
cards.searchQuery: placenta exchange nutrients gases waste mother fetus hormones

cards.title: What are the rhythmic waves of smooth muscle contraction that push food along the digestive tract called?
cards.body:
Peristalsis

Muscle behind the food contracts while muscle ahead relaxes, so the food moves forward, even if you are upside down.

Example: peristalsis carries swallowed food down the esophagus and moves material through the intestines.

Key idea: **peristalsis** is involuntary and uses smooth muscle.
cards.searchQuery: peristalsis smooth muscle waves digestive tract esophagus
